speaker: Anna Lembke
title: Overcome Addictions and Obsessions of All Kinds | Dr. Anna Lembke
question: In addiction medicine, if a patient uses multiple substances, do they need to abstain from all of them simultaneously to see clinical improvement?
guest: All reinforcing substances and behaviors work on the same final common pathway, and dopamine has become a kind of common currency for measuring the addictive potential of many different substances and behaviors. They all have their own unique chemical cascade, but they all ultimately release dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. Clinically speaking, you would think that if somebody was using nicotine, alcohol, and cannabis and was just willing to give up one of those, it wouldn't have a restorative impact because you've got the other things going on. But it turns out clinically what we see is even if they're only willing to give up nicotine, as long as they don't replace it with something else or escalate their cannabis or alcohol use, we see improvements. There are studies showing that for people addicted to alcohol and nicotine who give up both at the same time compared to those who only give up alcohol, the people who gave up both tend to have better outcomes, because you're not constantly pinging your reward pathway. We will also ask people to give up more than one substance if they're obviously paired, like coffee almost always followed by craving for a cigarette.

points.core: Quitting just one substance still yields clinical improvement despite shared dopamine pathways.
points.note: Accept: partial abstinence or quitting a single substance still improves outcomes even though addictive substances converge on the nucleus accumbens / dopamine reward pathway. Do not credit: claiming patients must quit every substance simultaneously or generic "any reduction helps" platitudes without the shared-pathway contrast.

points.core: Partial abstinence works only when patients avoid escalating their remaining substance use.
points.note: Accept: avoiding substitution, cross-addiction, or escalating remaining substances/behaviors. Do not credit: vague advice to "stay disciplined" or claiming substitution never occurs.

points.core: Quitting co-occurring addictions simultaneously produces stronger long-term outcomes than sequential cessation.
points.note: Accept: prospective evidence that quitting paired addictions like alcohol and nicotine together outperforms quitting only one. Do not credit: claiming quitting one substance is always better than quitting both, or both-sides hedging with no outcome distinction.

points.core: Clinicians require simultaneous abstinence whenever one substance reliably cues craving for another.
points.note: Accept: behaviorally paired or cue-linked substances (e.g., coffee triggering cigarette cravings) must be stopped together. Do not credit: generic mentions of triggers without linking cue-pairing to the decision to require multi-substance abstinence.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
No. Evidence and current guidelines support that clinical improvement does not require stopping every substance at once. Reducing or stopping even one substance, or simply using less, is associated with meaningful gains in health, functioning, and survival. For example, patients on methadone or buprenorphine for opioid use disorder benefit substantially (lower overdose and mortality risk) even if they continue using cannabis, stimulants, or other drugs, and ASAM guidance states that ongoing use of other substances is not a reason to withhold or discontinue that treatment. Likewise, reduced stimulant or alcohol use short of abstinence is linked to improved psychosocial and medical outcomes, and the FDA now accepts reduction in use as a valid treatment endpoint.

That said, treating co-occurring substance use concurrently is generally encouraged where the patient is willing. Smoking cessation during addiction treatment, for instance, does not jeopardize recovery and is associated with somewhat better long-term abstinence from other substances. Some combinations also carry specific risks worth prioritizing, such as opioids with benzodiazepines or alcohol.

In practice, goals are individualized and often sequential, guided by patient priorities and risk.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
No, patients do not need to abstain from all substances simultaneously to achieve meaningful clinical improvement. Modern addiction medicine, including guidance from the American Society of Addiction Medicine, favors harm reduction and stepwise care over all-or-nothing abstinence requirements. Stabilizing or reducing the highest-risk substance—for instance, treating opioid use disorder with buprenorphine or methadone—substantially lowers overdose mortality, infectious disease transmission, and hospitalizations, even if a patient continues using cannabis, stimulants, alcohol, or nicotine. Demanding immediate, total abstinence often drives patients from care and increases fatal relapse risk.

Still, ongoing polysubstance use warrants careful clinical management. Combinations like opioids with alcohol or benzodiazepines carry severe overdose risks, and secondary substance use can cue cravings or impair functioning. Conversely, when patients are ready, addressing co-occurring addictions concurrently—such as integrating tobacco cessation—often strengthens rather than destabilizes recovery. Clinicians therefore target the deadliest risks first while collaborating toward reduced harm or abstinence across other substances over time.

noweb.answer: No, patients who use multiple substances do not need to abstain from all of them simultaneously to achieve meaningful clinical improvement. Modern addiction medicine prioritizes harm reduction and low-barrier, patient-centered care over strict all-or-nothing abstinence requirements. Clinicians typically focus first on stabilizing the substance carrying the highest immediate risk of mortality or severe harm, such as illicit opioids or heavy alcohol use. For example, starting medications for opioid use disorder—such as buprenorphine or methadone—dramatically reduces overdose deaths and improves daily functioning even when a patient continues using stimulants, cannabis, or tobacco. Mandating total simultaneous abstinence as a condition of treatment often drives dropout and increases overdose risk. That said, ongoing polysubstance use still requires careful clinical management, especially when patients combine central nervous system depressants like opioids, alcohol, and benzodiazepines, or when one substance reliably triggers heavy use of another. Ultimately, reducing or stopping even a single high-risk substance produces substantial health benefits and often builds the stability needed to address remaining substances over time.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
No, they don't have to stop everything at once. Current addiction medicine generally doesn't treat simultaneous abstinence from all substances as a requirement for clinical improvement.

The evidence supports this in several ways. Patients on methadone or buprenorphine for opioid use disorder still get large reductions in overdose deaths and other harms even when they keep using cannabis or stimulants. Most guidelines advise against discharging patients for that kind of use. Reducing use without stopping completely, such as lowering heavy drinking days or cutting back on cocaine, is also linked to measurable gains in health, mood and functioning. Many clinicians work with patients on their priorities, usually starting with the substance causing the most harm, which helps keep people in treatment.

That said, treating several substances together can be useful. A Prochaska 2004 meta-analysis found that adding smoking cessation to addiction treatment was linked to better long-term abstinence from alcohol and other drugs, not worse. Some combinations also carry specific risks. Alcohol or benzodiazepines taken with opioids sharply raise overdose risk, so they deserve focused attention even when full abstinence isn't the immediate goal.

Stopping or even reducing use of a single substance—particularly the highest-risk one, such as opioids or alcohol—can substantially lower overdose risk, medical complications, and mortality while improving stability and quality of life. Because of this, clinicians generally take an individualized, harm-reduction approach: they prioritize immediate safety and the patient's own goals, treating the most harmful substance first or addressing substances stepwise, rather than requiring complete, simultaneous abstinence as a prerequisite for care or progress.

noweb.answer:
No, patients who use multiple substances do not need to abstain from all of them simultaneously to experience meaningful clinical improvement. In modern addiction medicine, treatment is increasingly guided by harm reduction and patient-centered goals rather than strict, all-or-nothing abstinence. Addressing the most harmful or life-threatening substance first—such as stabilizing opioid use disorder with medications like buprenorphine or methadone, even if the patient continues using cannabis, nicotine, or stimulants—can dramatically reduce overdose mortality, medical complications, and acute instability.

Reducing use or achieving abstinence from even one substance often improves physical health, psychiatric stability, treatment engagement, and daily functioning, which can build momentum for addressing other substances later. While concurrent use of certain substances—such as alcohol or benzodiazepines alongside opioids—carries significant safety risks that require careful clinical monitoring and management, demanding immediate, total abstinence from every substance can alienate patients and lead to treatment dropout. Tailoring treatment to prioritize the highest risks while supporting incremental progress typically yields better long-term outcomes.
